claim: Convergence-extension in embryos is controlled by chemical and mechanical signalling.
source: Convergence–extension in embryos is controlled by chemical and mechanical signalling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general background statement about convergence-extension processes.

claim: A key cellular process in convergence-extension is the exchange of neighbours via T1 transitions.
source: A key cellular process is the exchange of neighbours via T1 transitions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about cellular processes.

claim: The model produces active T1 events which act to elongate the tissue perpendicular to the main direction of tissue stress.
source: The model produces active T1 events, which act to elongate the tissue perpendicular to the main direction of tissue stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is an optimal range of mechanical stresses to trigger an active T1 event.
source: Using an idealised tissue patch comprising several active cells embedded in a matrix of passive hexagonal cells, we identified an optimal range of mechanical stresses to trigger an active T1 event.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations described in the abstract.

claim: Directed stresses generate tension chains in a realistic patch made entirely of active cells of random shapes.
source: We show that directed stresses also generate tension chains in a realistic patch made entirely of active cells of random shapes and leads to convergence–extension over a range of parameters.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations described in the abstract.

claim: Active intercalations can generate stress that activates T1 events in neighbouring cells.
source: Our findings show that active intercalations can generate stress that activates T1 events in neighbouring cells, resulting in tension-dependent tissue reorganisation, in qualitative agreement with experiments on gastrulation in chick embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model that is compared to experimental data.

claim: Directed cell intercalation is a major mechanism driving large-scale tissue shape changes in both epithelial and mesenchymal tissues.
source: Directed cell intercalation is a major mechanism driving large-scale tissue shape changes both in epithelial and mesenchymal tissues (Huebner and Wallingford, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huebner and Wallingford, 2018.

claim: Convergent extension is the narrowing and lengthening of epithelial tissues resulting from cell intercalations.
source: The narrowing and lengthening of epithelial tissues resulting from such intercalations, known as convergent extension (Keller et al., 2000), underlie germband extension in Drosophila (Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006), as well as primitive streak formation in the chick embryo (Voiculescu et al., 2007; Rozbicki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations defining and providing examples of convergent extension.

claim: Cell intercalations facilitate coordinated movements of hundreds of thousands of cells in two counter-rotating millimetre-scale cell flows during primitive streak formation in the chick embryo.
source: In the latter, cell intercalations facilitate coordinated movements of hundreds of thousands of cells in two counter-rotating millimetre-scale cell flows that drive the formation of the primitive streak at the site where the flows meet (Rozbicki et al., 2015; Saadaoui et al., 2020; Serrano Nájera and Weijer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on chick embryo development.

claim: During intercalation, cells pull against each other in order to exchange their neighbours.
source: Unlike cell migration (Alert and Trepat, 2020), which typically involves a significant contribution from crawling against a substrate such as the extracellular matrix, during intercalation, cells pull against each other in order to exchange their neighbours (Huebner and Wallingford, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations distinguishing intercalation from migration.

claim: The T1 transition requires a carefully coordinated shrinking and subsequent expansion of cell-cell interfaces.
source: This is a complex, active process that requires a carefully coordinated shrinking and subsequent expansion of cell–cell interfaces, known as the T1 transition (Kong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2017.

claim: During germband extension in Drosophila, dorsal-ventral oriented junctions shrink and new junctions are generated in anterior-posterior direction.
source: The widely studied morphological process of germband extension in Drosophila involves directed cell intercalations in the ventral ectoderm, where during the associated T1 events dorsal–ventral (DV)-oriented junctions shrink and new junctions are generated in anterior–posterior (AP) direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: The contraction of DV-oriented junctions correlates with increased accumulation of apical myosin II in these junctions that can form supercellular cables.
source: The contraction of DV-oriented junctions has been shown to correlate with increased accumulation of apical myosin II in these junctions that can form supercellular cables in aligned junctions (Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The extension of new junctions has been associated with the activity of medial myosin.
source: The extension of new junctions has been associated with the activity of medial myosin (Rauzi et al., 2010; Collinet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Myosin-rich DV-oriented junctions are under higher tension than AP junctions in the Drosophila ventral ectoderm.
source: Laser ablation experiments in the ventral ectoderm have shown that the myosin-rich DV-oriented junctions are under higher tension than AP junctions (Rauzi et al., 2008; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Collinet et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to laser ablation experiments.

claim: Myosin can be recruited to junctions in response to increased tension, demonstrating the existence of mechanical feedback.
source: aspiration and optical tweezing and optogenetic experiments have shown that myosin can be recruited to junctions in response to increased tension in these junctions, demonstrating the existence of mechanical feedback (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Clément et al., 2017; Gustafson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies using various techniques.

claim: Myosin accumulates on apical junctions in response to mechanical stretching of the Drosophila wing disk.
source: This is in agreement with observations in the Drosophila wing disk when it has recently been shown that myosin accumulates on apical junctions in response to mechanical stretching of the disk (Duda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duda et al., 2019.

claim: The distribution of apical myosin can accurately predict the observed tissue flow patterns during germband extension.
source: It has recently been shown that the distribution of apical myosin can accurately predict the observed tissue flow patterns during germband extension (Streichan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Streichan et al., 2018.

claim: The mechanism by which the anisotropic distribution of myosin cables is initially generated during germband extension is unresolved.
source: However, an as yet unresolved question is by which mechanism the anisotropic distribution of myosin cables is initially generated.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field.

claim: The anisotropic distribution of myosin is thought to depend on the family of Toll receptors under the control of pair rule genes.
source: It is thought to depend on the family of Toll receptors under the control of pair rule genes (Paré et al., 2014) and their interactions with an adhesion G protein0coupled receptor (Lavalou et al., 2021) that could generate asymmetries in cells and can possibly signal to Rho-kinase and myosin; however, the precise molecular details remain to be resolved.
evidence: This is supported by citations but noted as incompletely understood.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the DV junctional strain rate gradient and the junctional myosin recruitment rate gradient during germband extension.
source: Recently, a strong correlation between the DV junctional strain rate gradient and the junctional myosin recruitment rate gradient, both high at the ventral side, has been observed (Gustafson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gustafson et al., 2022.

claim: Myosin anisotropy may arise in response to extrinsic forces such as those generated by mesoderm invagination of the ventral furrow.
source: This has led to the renewed suggestion that the myosin anisotropy may arise in response to extrinsic forces, such as those generated by the mesoderm invagination of the ventral furrow (Butler et al., 2009), a process that starts somewhat before germband extension and in combination with other extrinsic events such as posterior hindgut invagination, and other geometric constraints could drive germband extension (Collinet et al., 2015; Gehrels et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations and presented as a hypothesis.

claim: Directed intercalations of mesendoderm precursors in a sickle-shaped region drive the tissue flows underlying primitive streak formation in the chick embryo.
source: Experiments in the chick embryo showed that directed intercalations of mesendoderm precursors located in a sickle-shaped region in the posterior of the epiblast drive the tissue flows underlying the formation of the primitive streak (Voiculescu et al., 2007; Rozbicki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The sickle-shaped mesendoderm precursor region contracts along its long axis towards the AP midline and extends along this midline in anterior direction to form the primitive streak.
source: This sickle-shaped mesendoderm precursor region contracts along its long axis towards the AP midline of the embryo and extends along this midline in anterior direction to form the primitive streak.
evidence: This describes the morphological process observed in chick embryos.

claim: The directions of intercalations are aligned along the long axis of the mesendoderm sickle in the direction of contraction and correlate with the direction and magnitude of the anisotropic strain rate component.
source: Measurements of the directions of intercalations show that they are aligned along the long axis of the mesendoderm sickle in the direction of the contraction of the sickle and correlate well with the direction and magnitude of the anisotropic strain rate component (Rozbicki et al., 2015; Chuai et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental measurements.

claim: Directed intercalations in the chick embryo are mediated by supercellular myosin cables in aligned junctions in the direction of intercalation.
source: These directed intercalations are mediated by super cellular myosin cables in aligned junctions in the direction of intercalation (Rozbicki et al., 2015; Saadaoui et al., 2020; Serrano Nájera and Weijer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: The onset of tissue motion starts near the central midline of the sickle and rapidly extends outwards to more lateral regions, suggesting the existence of an outward-propagating signal.
source: The onset of tissue motion starts near the central midline of the sickle and then rapidly extends outwards to more lateral regions, suggesting the existence of an outward-propagating signal (Rozbicki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from experiments that leads to an inference about signal propagation.

claim: Intercalating cells in the chick embryo undergo characteristic elongation in the direction of intercalation around the time of onset of motion.
source: Furthermore, the intercalating cells go through a characteristic elongation in the direction of intercalation around the time of the onset of motion, which disappears when the epiblast tissue flows pickup speed.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments on chick embryos.

claim: Long-range mechanical signals coordinate cell intercalations at large scales in the chick embryo.
source: These observations, coupled with the fact that the chick embryo epiblast contains more than 60,000 cells at the onset of gastrulation requiring coordination of cell intercalation over large distances, led us to suggest that long-range mechanical signals coordinate the intercalations in the large scale (Rozbicki et al., 2015; Serrano Nájera and Weijer, 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on observations and cited work.

claim: Local contraction of a junction increases tension in aligned junctions of neighbouring cells, activating a mechanical feedback process that results in their contraction.
source: More specifically, Rozbicki et al., 2015; Serrano Nájera and Weijer, 2020 proposed that local contraction of a junction would, through an increase in tension in aligned junctions of neighbouring cells, activate a mechanical feedback process in those junctions, in turn, resulting in their contraction.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from cited work.

claim: The orientation and alignment of myosin cables correlate well with the anisotropic component of the strain rate tensor in chick embryos.
source: The orientation and alignment of the myosin cables, however, correlate well with the anisotropic component of the strain rate tensor (Rozbicki et al., 2015; Chuai et al., 2023), making it likely that a tension-dependent recruitment of myosin occurs in chick embryos.
evidence: This is supported by citations and leads to an inference about tension-dependent myosin recruitment.

claim: The viscoelastic nature of cell-cell junctions is essential for an active T1 event.
source: Our analysis indicates that the viscoelastic nature of the cell–cell junctions is essential for an active T1 event, in agreement with studies on ratcheting during junction contractions (Clément et al., 2017; Staddon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis supported by citations.

claim: The junction is viscoelastic as established by pull-release optical tweezer experiments on cell-cell junctions in Drosophila and chick embryos.
source: The junction is viscoelastic, as established by pull-release optical tweezer experiments on cell–cell junctions in Drosophila and chick embryos (Clément et al., 2017; Ferro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The junction can generate tension via the action of myosin motor minifilaments that slide actin filaments against each other.
source: The junction can generate tension via the action of myosin motor minifilaments that slide actin filaments against each other.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myosin function.

claim: There is self-amplifying feedback due to the exponentially decreasing unbinding rate of myosin motors with tension in the junction.
source: There is self-amplifying feedback due to the exponentially decreasing unbinding rate of myosin motors with tension in the junction (Veigel et al., 2003; Kovács et al., 2007; Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in figures.

claim: Epithelial tissues and early-stage embryos are under mechanical tension as revealed by tissue and cell junction cutting and tweezing experiments.
source: Furthermore, epithelial tissues, and early-stage embryos, in particular, are under mechanical tension as revealed by tissue and cell junction cutting and tweezing experiments (Clément et al., 2017; Ferro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: There is positive feedback between mechanical tension and activity resulting from the assumption that myosin association rate is independent of tension while dissociation rate decays exponentially with it.
source: Therefore, there is positive feedback between mechanical tension and activity, which results from the assumption that the myosin association rate is independent of tension while the dissociation rate decays exponentially with it.
evidence: This is an inference from the model structure.

claim: Applying small external forces leads to an expanding junction, while increasing the force leads to junction shrinking due to increased bound myosin motors.
source: That is, applying small external forces will lead to an expanding junction. Increasing the force, however, leads to the junction shrinking due to the increase of bound myosin motors.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-junction model analysis.

claim: An initial myosin pulse applied to the central junction of a chain causes it to contract, and the contraction activates contractions of neighbouring junctions, leading to shrinking of the entire chain.
source: An initial myosin pulse applied to the central junction causes it to contract. The contraction of the central junction activates contractions of the neighbouring junctions, leading to shrinking of the entire chain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B from model simulations.

claim: The contraction rate strongly depends on the timescale of viscoelastic relaxation in the junction.
source: Finally, the contraction rate strongly depends on the timescale of viscoelastic relaxation in the junction.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The vertex model is able to capture both fluid and solid behaviours of epithelial tissues, including some aspects of viscoelastic rheology.
source: The appeal of the vertex model is that it is able to capture both fluid and solid behaviours of epithelial tissues, including some aspects of the viscoelastic rheology (Tong et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on vertex models.

claim: The central T1 and subsequent T1 events lead to substantial convergence-extension flow.
source: Together, the central T1 and the subsequent T1 events lead to substantial convergence–extension flow as can be seen qualitatively in the shape of the region formed by the 14 central and buffer cells (Figure 2, medium and dark grey).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 from model simulations.

claim: The orientation of the central T1 transition in the optimal region is highly symmetric, with the shrinking junction being very close to horizontal and the expanding junction very close to vertical.
source: One can immediately observe that the transition is highly symmetric, with the orientation of the shrinking (disappearing) junction being very close to horizontal, and the expanding (appearing) junction very close to vertical.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D from model simulations.

claim: Unlike in the hexagonal patch, there is no clear threshold for active T1 transitions in the random patch.
source: Unlike in the case of the active inclusion in a hexagonal passive patch, there is no clear threshold for active T1 transitions.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations of the random patch.

claim: There is evidence of serial active T1 transitions along tension chains in the random patch.
source: This suggests cooperative rearrangements in the tissue, and we indeed see evidence of serial active T1 transitions along tension chains (Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—video 2 from model simulations.

claim: The individual junction feedback mechanism together with mechanical propagation of myosin activation is a key ingredient in the formation of myosin cables observed during convergence-extension flow.
source: This suggests that the individual junction feedback mechanism together with mechanical (as opposed to chemical) propagation of myosin activation is a key ingredient in the formation of the myosin cables that have been observed to accompany convergence–extension flow in chick embryo gastrulation (Rozbicki et al., 2015) and in Drosophila germ band extension (Jacinto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results compared to experimental observations.

claim: At longer times, the pronounced orientation of myosin and tension decreases but does not disappear entirely, and convergence-extension stops.
source: At longer times, the pronounced orientation of myosin and tension decreases (but does not disappear entirely), and convergence–extension stops (see 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations of the random patch.

claim: The convergence-extension process is accompanied by active T1 events that predominately occur perpendicular to the direction of the external pulling.
source: The convergence–extension process is accompanied by active T1 events that predominately occur perpendicular to the direction of the external pulling, as shown in the orientational histogram (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B from model simulations.

claim: The random patch undergoes substantial convergence-extension over a range of activities.
source: It is evident that like the hexagonal case, the random patch undergoes substantial convergence–extension over a range of activities.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C from model simulations.

claim: The convergence-extension process is accompanied by spatially anisotropic distribution of myosin, mechanical stress, and cell shapes.
source: The process in accompanied by spatially anisotropic distribution of myosin, mechanical stress, and cell shapes (Figure 7D), which we measured through the eigenvalues of the myosin (Equation 26) and tension (Equation 25) tensors, and the eigenvalues of the shape tensor (Equation 20).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D from model simulations.

claim: Cells undergoing directed intercalations in the chick embryo are characterised by an anisotropic cell shape and an anisotropic distribution of active myosin II in their cell junctions, organised in supercellular chains.
source: These cells undergoing directed intercalations are characterised by an anisotropic cell shape and an anisotropic distribution of active myosin II in their cell junctions, organised in supercellular chains of variable length (Figure 8A and A'; Rozbicki et al., 2015; Chuai et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 8A and A'.

claim: Both myosin and cell shapes exhibit a clear anisotropy along the lateral-medial axis of the mesendoderm precursor domain in the chick embryo.
source: Both the myosin (green) and cell shapes exhibit a clear anisotropy (indicated by green arrows) along the lateral–medial axis of the mesendoderm precursor domain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A from experimental data.

claim: The anisotropy in the chick embryo remains constant at around 20% and its direction is at an angle close to 90°, along the sickle and orthogonal to the streak.
source: The anisotropy remains constant at around 20% and its direction is at the angle close to 90°, that is, along the sickle and orthogonal to the streak (Figure 8C', green arrow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C' from experimental data analysis.

claim: There is a pronounced spatial pattern to the flow direction in the chick embryo, pointing towards the streak and parallel to the direction of anisotropy on outer parts of the sickle, and orthogonal to the sickle in the middle.
source: There is a pronounced spatial pattern to its direction, pointing towards the streak and parallel to the direction of anisotropy on outer parts of the sickle, and orthogonal to the sickle and its orientation in the middle of the sickle (Figure 8C', red arrows).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C' from experimental data analysis.

claim: The magnitude of flow peaks in the middle part of the sickle in the chick embryo.
source: At the same time, the magnitude of flow peaks in the middle part of the sickle.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C from experimental data analysis.

claim: An isotropic region anterior to the streak shows non-directional intercalations and absence of tissue deformation.
source: For comparison, we show the behaviour in an isotropic region anterior to the streak that shows non-directional intercalations and absence of tissue deformation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 3C, and Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures from experimental data analysis.

claim: The anisotropy of myosin distribution is induced by anisotropic mechanical tension in the model.
source: First, the anisotropy of myosin distribution is induced by anisotropic mechanical tension.
evidence: This is a key feature of the model described in the Discussion.

claim: Active contractions are triggered by tension-sensitive accumulation in the model.
source: Second, active contractions are triggered by tension-sensitive accumulation.
evidence: This is a key feature of the model described in the Discussion.

claim: The feedback loop between tension and myosin motor activity leads to contraction against and extension perpendicular to tension.
source: The feedback loop between tension and myosin motor activity leads to contraction against and extension perpendicular to tension.
evidence: This is a key finding of the model described in the Discussion.

claim: This cellular mechanism has been suggested to be driving the tissue flows during primitive streak formation in avian embryos.
source: This cellular mechanism has been suggested to be driving the tissue flows during primitive streak formation in avian embryos (Rozbicki et al., 2015), where there is no clear evidence of chemical prepatterning.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and noted as a hypothesis.

claim: It is plausible that the symmetry breaking event that induces the initial myosin anisotropy occurs as a result of anisotropic tension combined with cell differentiation early in development.
source: Although it is yet to be experimentally confirmed, it is plausible that the symmetry breaking event that induces the initial myosin anisotropy occurs as a result of anisotropic tension combined with cell differentiation early in development.
evidence: This is presented as a plausible hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: Gdf3 is expressed in the sickle-shaped region in the posterior epiblast of the chick embryo and is believed to play a role in triggering the contractions that initiate the large-scale tissue flows.
source: For example, in the chick embryo, Gdf3 is expressed in the sickle-shaped region in the posterior epiblast, and it is believed to play a role in triggering the contractions that initiate the large-scale tissue flows that subsequently lead to the formation of the primitive streak (Serrano Nájera and Weijer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Once the process has been initiated, chemical anisotropy emerges spontaneously and there is no need to impose it.
source: The key conclusion of this study is that once the process has been initiated, chemical anisotropy emerges spontaneously and there is no need to impose it.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: The model loses coherence after several T1 events, resulting in biologically implausible tissue shapes.
source: Although the model investigated here generates active T1 events, the process loses coherence after several T1 events, resulting in biologically implausible tissue shapes.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model discussed in the Discussion.

claim: One source of instability is likely that the post-T1 expansion of the junction is not properly captured by the model and requires additional sources of activity to be considered.
source: One source of instability is likely that the post-T1 expansion of the junction, currently effectively modelled as a passive process, is not properly captured by the model and requires additional sources of activity to be considered.
evidence: This is a speculation about model limitations in the Discussion.

claim: The single-junction model shares common features with the model of Dierkes et al., 2014.
source: The single-junction model shares a lot of common features with the model of Dierkes et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work in the Discussion.

claim: The key difference from Dierkes et al., 2014 is a different myosin-tension feedback mechanism and that the dashpot was replaced with a Maxwell element.
source: The key difference, however, is a different myosin–tension feedback mechanism and that the dashpot in Dierkes et al., 2014 was replaced with a Maxwell element.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work in the Discussion.

claim: Laser tweezer measurements showed that cellular junctions behave as a Maxwell viscoelastic material.
source: This was inspired by laser tweezer measurements of the response of cell–cell junctions in the Drosophila embryo to applied pulling force (Clément et al., 2017) which showed that the cellular junctions behave as a Maxwell viscoelastic material.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The presence of an elastic spring attached to the dashpot introduces a viscoelastic timescale, which leads to the suppression of the oscillatory behaviour seen in Dierkes et al., 2014.
source: The presence of an elastic spring attached to the dashpot introduces a viscoelastic timescale, which leads to the suppression of the oscillatory behaviour seen in Dierkes et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work explaining differences in behavior.

claim: The key for the mechanism of the active T1 transition is that there is increased contractile activity in response to external mechanical tension, without the need to specify its precise molecular origin.
source: The key for the mechanism of the active T1 transition studied here is that there is increased contractile activity in response to external mechanical tension, without the need to specify its precise molecular origin.
evidence: This is a statement about the generality of the model mechanism.

claim: Nonmuscle myosin II has actin association rates that are tension-independent but exhibits tension-dependent dissociation.
source: The reason, however, to consider tension-dependent unbinding is because the nonmuscle myosin II, which is the primary molecular motor that drives contractions in early embryonic tissues, is known to have actin association rates that are tension-independent, but exhibits tension-dependent dissociation (Kovács et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Pulling experiments on suspended cultured MDCK-II cells and on the Drosophila wing disk do not show any topological transitions even for strains that exceed 50%.
source: Finally, we remark that pulling experiments on suspended cultured Madine Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK-II) cells (Harris et al., 2012) and on the Drosophila wing disk (Duda et al., 2019) do not show any topological transitions even for strains that exceed 50%.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: It is unlikely that the mechanism proposed in this study would apply to MDCK cells or fly wing disk tissues.
source: While it is possible that T1 transitions would appear given sufficiently long time, it is unlikely that the mechanism proposed in this study would apply to these tissues.
evidence: This is an inference about the applicability of the model.

claim: MDCK cells are transformed cells derived from adult tissues and likely not comparable to embryonic tissues that need to undergo large-scale highly coordinated shape changes.
source: This is not unexpected since MDCK cells are transformed cells derived from adult tissues and likely not comparable to embryonic tissues that need to undergo large-scale highly coordinated shape changes involving massive cell rearrangements.
evidence: This is reasoning about why the model may not apply to certain tissues.

claim: Models that share the common assumption of a feedback between activity and mechanical tension are able to describe a range of markedly different biological processes in different organisms.
source: We conclude by observing that it is remarkable that models that share the common assumption of a feedback between activity and mechanical tension are able to describe a range of markedly different biological processes in different organisms.
evidence: This is a concluding observation about the generality of the modeling approach.

claim: There is a set of universal physical mechanisms that govern tissue-scale behaviours.
source: Although the details depend on the specific biological system and its molecular details, this suggests that there is a set of universal physical mechanisms that govern tissue-scale behaviours.
evidence: This is a concluding speculation about universal mechanisms.
